P-459 
Stiff Person Syndrome (SPS): A Pediatric Case Report 
N.S. Shah .1 , A. Hahn 2, B. Banwell 1. 1Toronto, Canada; 2London, 
Canada 
Introduction: SPS is a rare disorder characterized by fluctuating muscle 
rigidity and spasms. Most patients present in adulthood. We report a case 
with onset at 8 years, review of reported pediatric cases, and discuss 
various therapeutic modalities. 
Clinical evulation: A previously healthy, athletic 8 year old girl had onset 
of severe episodes of pain in lower back and legs. Recurrent, episodic mus- 
cle stiffness precipitated by loud noise and tactile stimulation lasting 3 to 
5 minutes, occurred multiple times per day. Examination during episodes 
revealed muscle stiffness with extreme pain with hyperreflexia. Reduced 
lumbar extension and subjective stiffness in lower paraspinal muscles 
without myotonia was evident between attacks. MRI head, CSF stud- 
ies, evoked potentials, and electromyography (performed when asymp- 
tomatic) were normal. Serum studies performed by the Mayo Clinic 
demonstrated GAD-65 (glutamic acid decarboxylase) antibody titres of 
0.13(normal = 0.02). Serum glucose and thyroid function were normal. 
Treatment: High dose corticosteroids significantly improved muscle 
spasms during attacks. The frequency of attacks was markedly reduced 
with monthly IVIg infusions and muscle stiffness has improved on main- 
tenance regime of Tizanidine and Gabapentin. 
Discussion: SPS is presumed to have an autoimmune pathogenesis, based 
on presence of GAD autoantibodies and association with other autoim- 
mune or paraneoplastic disorders. SPS is extremely rare in the pediatric 
population. The 8 cases described in the literature will be reviewed. The 
management of the present case highlights the need for multisymptomatic 
therapy. 
P-460 
Monomelic Amyotrophy of the Lower Extremity: A Report of 15 
Cases 
H.G. Stewart*, A. Eisen, M. Mezei. Vancouver, British Columbia, 
Canada 
Objective: To describe 15 consecutive cases (14 male) of monomelic 
amyotrophy of the lower extremity(MALE) observed over 15 years by 
one examiner. 
Methods: Patient, chart and literature review. 
Results: The mean age of onset of symptoms was 30 years (range: 10-50). 
The mean duration of symptoms was 8 years at last follow-up. In half of 
the cases, muscle wasting or abnormal gait was noted first by individuals 
other than the patient. Wasting was most marked in the posterior and 
anterior compartment muscles. Absent ankle jerks and pes cavus were 
common in the affected leg. EMG showed mixed patterns of acute and 
chronic denervation in both clinically involved and non-involved muscles. 
Spinal cord MRI, CT scans and myelograms were unremarkable. One 
patient's brother and daughter had amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), 
the daughter confirmed to be homozygous for the D90A Cu/Zn superoxide 
dismutase (SOD 1) mutation. 
Conclusions: Monomelic amyotrophy of the lower extremity is a rare dis- 
order characterized by wasting and weakness of a single lower extremity 
with insidious onset and slow progression that may arrest spontaneously. 
Function is relatively well maintained. Sensory abnormalities and long-

tract signs are rare. The etiopathogenesis and relationship of MALE to 
other disorders of motor neurons is poorly understood. 
Muscle Biology/In Vitro studies 
P-461 
Phosphorylation Regulates the Subcellular Localization of 
Syntrophin/Diacylglycerol Kinase-~ Complexes in Skeletal Muscle 
Cells 
Hanan Abramovici* 1, Matthew K. Topham 2, Stephen Gee 1. 
1Department of Cellular and Molecular Medicine, Center for 
Neuromuscular Disease, University of Ottawa, Ottawa, Ontario K1H 
8M5 Canada; :Huntsman Cancer Institute and Department of Internal 
Medicine, University of Utah, Salt Lake City, Utah 84112, USA 
Syntrophins are a family of structurally related proteins with multiple pro- 
tein interaction motifs, allowing them to simultaneously bind dystrophin 
family members and signaling proteins. At the membrane of normal 
skeletal muscle fibers, syntrophins associate with diacylglycerol kinase-~ 
(DGK-~), an enzyme that converts the lipid second messenger diacyl- 
glycerol (DAG) to phosphatidic acid (PA). However, in the dystrophin- 
deficient mdx mouse, sarcolemmal syntrophins and DGK-~ are markedly 
reduced, raising the possibility that mislocalization of DGK-~ in skele- 
tal muscle contributes to the pathogenesis of muscular dystrophies. To 
study the molecular mechanisms that regulate the membrane localization 
of DGK-~ and syntrophins in muscle, we transiently transfected C2C12 
cells with epitope tagged versions of these proteins. In C2 myoblasts over- 
expressing HA-tagged wild type DGK- G the enzyme was primarily cy- 
toplasmic. In contrast, myc-tagged cd-syntrophin was mostly membrane 
associated. In cotransfected cells, both proteins were colocalized in the cy- 
tosol, suggesting syntrophins sequester DGK-~ away from plasma mem- 
brane DAG. On the other hand, a constitutively phosphorylated DGK- 
mutant was associated with cd-syntrophin at the plasma membrane. 
We propose that phosphorylation regulates the membrane localization of 
DGK-~/syntrophin complexes in muscle, which may be critical for the 
control of DGK-~ activity and the regulation of both DAG and PA signal- 
ing pathways. 
P-462 
Mitochondrial Ca 2+ Signaling in Dystrophic Myotubes 
Olivier Basset*, Katy Bernard, Val rie Nicolas-M tral, Corinne Challet, 
Timo M. Buetler, Urs T. Ruegg. Group of Pharmacology, School of 
Pharmacy, University of Lausanne, Switzerland 
Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy (DMD) is an X-linked recessive genetic 
disease caused by the absence of dystrophin, a protein linking the ex- 
tracellular matrix via a transmembrane glycoprotein complex to the cy- 
toskeleton. Previous work has demonstrated that, in DMD skeletal muscle 
cells, the concentration of cytosolic Ca 2+ is increased and might mediate 
cell death. Using the Ca 2+ sensitive photoprotein aequorin specifically 
targeted to mitochondria we have found that mitochondrial Ca 2+ concen- 
trations ([Ca2+]m) are lower in myotubes derived from the soleus muscle 
of the mdx mouse (a model of DMD) than in soleus C57 control cells. 
Treatment with creatine increases [Ca2+]m exclusively in mdx cells and 
has no effect in C57 cells showing a preferential disease specific action 
of creatine. The inhibitor of the sarcoplasmic reticulum Ca2+-ATPase 
thapsigargin blocks the KCl-induced [Ca2+]m peak, suggesting that close 
contacts between both organelles exist permitting Ca 2+ exchanges during 
KC1 depolarization. We have now overexpressed the anti-apoptotic pro-

tein Bcl-2 in our mdx and C57 myotubes and found that Bcl-2 decreases 
the [Ca2+]m response to KC1 depolarization, suggesting that Bcl-2 might 
control cellular calcium regulation via [Ca 2+ ]m in these myotubes and that 
this may be responsible for its anti-apoptotic effect. 
Supported by the Association Fran aise contre les Myopathies (AFM) and 
the Swiss National Science Foundation.

P-463 
A Sequential Expression of Potassium and Calcium Channel is 
Required for the Fusion of Human Myoblasts 
L. Bernheim*, J.-H. Liu, P. Bijlenga, J. Fischer-Lougheed, E. Espinos, 
C.R. Bader. Geneva, Switzerland 
Myoblast fusion is essential to skeletal muscle development and repair, 
andunderstanding this process is important for myoblast-based grafts or 
gene therapies. Fusion between myoblasts, or between myoblasts and 
myotubes, is known to be a calcium-dependent process requiring a cal- 
cium influx. We characterized the molecular mechanisms involved in this 
process in clonal cultures of human myoblasts. Our results suggest that 
the membrane potential and the biophysical properties of specific ionic 
channels are important actors in the fusion process. Electrophysiological 
recordings, RNase protection assays, and anti-RNA expression vectors 
were used to establish the molecular identity of the involved channels. 
Specifically, we found that human myoblasts hyperpolarize before fusion 
through the sequential expression of two potassium channels: an ether- - 
go-go and a Kir2.1 inward rectifier. This hyperpolarization is a prerequisite 
for fusion to occur. Then, just before fusion, an alpha-lH T-type calcium 
channel is expressed. We propose that the purpose of the hyperpolarization 
is to set the membrane potential in a range at which a window calcium 
current through the alpha-lH T- channels is activated. In this model, the 
window current would generate the fusion-required calcium entry. Similar 
mechanisms could operate in other cell types of which differentiation 
implicates membrane hyperpolarization. 
P-464 
The Expression of Transglutaminase in the Formation of Myotubes 
Y.-C. Choi* t, y. Yang2. 1Seoul, Korea; 2Deajoen, Korea 
Objective: Tranglutaminase (TG) is a calcium dependent cross-linking 
enzymes which form an isopeptide N-(gamma-glutamyl) lysine bond be- 
tween peptide bound glutamine and lysine residues. This enzyme stabi- 
lize intra- and extra-cellular proteins into macromolecular assemblies in 
a variety of essential physiological purposes such as apoptosis, wound 
healing, cell differentiation and cell proliferation. Recent our study has 
documented abnormally increased TG expression in myopathies (Choi 
YC et. al., J Bioi Chem 2000; 275:8703-10). To investigate its possible 
participation in the formation of myotuhes, we investigated the expression 
of TG on myoblasts and myotubes. 
Methods: Immunocytochemical staining was performed using polyclonal 
antibodies against TG on C2C12 cells, a mouse myoblast cell. The expres- 
sion of TG mRNA by RT-PCR and total TG enzyme activity were also 
determined on myotubes differentiated from C2C 12 myoblasts. 
Results: The expression of TG mRNA and total enzyme activity was 
increased on the myotubes compared with the myoblasts. Immunocyto- 
chemically, TG was also expressed on the myoblasts and myotubes during 
differentiation. 
Conclusion: TG expression during formation of myotubes, activated by 
an increase in the concentration of intracellular Ca2+, plays an important 
role in stabilizing the cytoskeletal network of developing myotubes. 
P-465 
Myod-Forced Myogenesis. Making Muscle - New Applications for 
Research and Prenatal Diagnosis of Muscle Disease 
Sandra T. Cooper*, H.P. Lo, B. Ilkowski, J.D. Yates, K.N. North. 
Institute for Neuromuscular Research, Clinical Sciences, The Children's

Hospital at Westmead, Locked Bag 4001, Westmead, NSW 2145, Sydney, 
Australia 
MyoD is one of four "master" myogenic determination factors, charac- 
terised by their ability to induce myogenic conversion when expressed 
in non-muscle cells 1. Using an adenoviral vector encoding MyoD 2, we 
have established MyoD-forced myogenesis in our laboratory and have 
developed it for use in a variety of diagnostic and research applications. 
MyoD-forced myogenesis means that we can use patient non-muscle cells 
(such as skin fibroblasts) as a source of "muscle cells" to examine the 
cellular consequences of disease-causing mutations. This technology pro- 
vides muscle-specific cDNA for mutation analysis (presenting significant 
advantages over screening genomic DNA), mutant protein for biochemi- 
cal analysis and patient muscle cells to examine during differentiation and 
maturation. MyoD-forced myogenesis also provides a means for prenatal 
diagnosis of Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD), and potentially other 
muscle disorders that resuk from a deficiency or clearly abnormal form 
of a muscle-specific protein. This study has characterised the myogenic 
differentiation and muscle-specific protein expression in MyoD-generated 
myotubes, particularly with respect to members of the dystrophin complex 
implicated in muscular dystrophy. We have analysed protein expression 
by immunocytochemistry and western blot and compared the time-course 
of gene expression to results obtained for C2C12 cells. We are also con- 
ducting a clinical trial to determine the sensitivity and specificity of this 
technology to provide prenatal diagnosis for families with DMD in cases 
where genetic diagnosis is uninformative. 
References 
[1] Davis, R.L., Weintraub, H., Lassar, A.B. (1987. Cell 51,987-1000. 
[2] Murray, C.E., Kay, M.A., Bartosek, T., Hauschka, S.D., Schwartz, 
S.M. (1996). J Clin Invest 98, 2209-2217. 
P-466 
Activation of Satellite Cells by Stretching Single Isolated Muscle 
Fibers 
A.C. Dyck*, J.E. Anderson. University of Manitoba, Winnipeg, Canada 
Satellite cells are located between external lamina and sarcolemma of 
skeletal muscle fibers. Normally quiescent, they are activated in vivo by 
injury, disease, stretch and exercise. Activated cells leave quiescence and 
become mitotically active and motile. We tested the hypothesis that satel- 
lite cells on single fibers would be activated by stretching in vitro. Fibers 
were isolated from normal mouse flexor digitorum brevis muscles, plated 
in flexible or rigid wells, and cultured overnight in serum replacement 
media (CSR2). Activation was marked by DNA synthesis, indicated by 
incorporated bromodeoxyuridine (BrdU) and visualized by immunostain- 
ing (BrdU+ cells/fiber). Fibers were stretched using a FlexCell system. 
BrdU was then added (0 time) and fibers were subjected to stretching at 4 
cycles per minute for 0-3 hours, then maintained until 24hr. Control fibers 
did not stretch. From 0-3 cells were BrdU+ on a single fiber. Satellite cell 
activation was stimulated in vitro by stretching (p<0.02, ANOVA) and 
had increased over controls at 2 hours (p<0.05). There was no further in- 
crease after 2 hours. Results suggest that the single fiber model is valuable 
for further study of signaling during stretch-induced activation. Satellite 
cells on fibers were maintained as quiescent, and when subjected to a 2hr 
stretch were triggered to enter mitotic events. 
Supported by MDA 
P-467

Muscle Regeneration Capacity of Myogenic Progenitors Identified 
by CD34 and SCA-1 Expression 
R. Jankowski*, B. Deasy, B. Cao, C. Gates, J. Greenberger, J. Huard. 
Pittsburgh, USA 
Objective: In order to utilize myogenic progenitors for cell therapies 
we must be able to identify and isolate reliable donor cell populations. 
The preplate isolation technique has been previously used to separate 
myogenic populations based on their variable adhesion characteristics. 
We set out to further understand this separation process and investigate the 
use of surface proteins to identify progenitors with enhanced regeneration 
capabilities. 
Methods: Based on previous studies, we investigated Sca-1 and CD34 
expression on myogenic populations with late adhesion characteristics and 
used cell sorting to purify fractions based on expression of these proteins. 
We compared the regeneration efficiency of these sorted progenitors, as 
well as those displaying early adhesion characteristics, by quantifying

$80 Wednesday, July 10, 2002 Poster Presentations 
their ability to restore dystrophin following transplantation into allogenic 
mdx host muscle. 
Results: CD34-expressing populations exhibited significant improve- 
ments in dystrophin restoration compared to both their CD34-negative 
counterparts and early adhering populations. This restoration ability was 
found to correspond to level of myogenic commitment, defined by myo- 
genic regulatory factor expression, and rate and degree of cell fusion of 
each population. 
Conclusions: These results demonstrate the ability to separate definable 
populations of myogenic progenitors with predictable regeneration effi- 
ciencies based upon basic characterization of both cell phenotype and 
fusion characteristics. 
P-468 
Expression Patterns of Cytokine mRNA in Human Fetal and Adult 
Myoblast and Human Skletal Muscle Cell Line 
I.S. Joo*, Y.B. Lee, H.S. Choi, K.Y Kim, S.U. Kim. Suwon, Korea 
Objective: To investigate whether expression patterns of cyokine mRNA 
differ across cultured human fetal and adult myoblasts and a human skele- 
tal muscle cell line (SKM14) that we developed. 
Methods: The amount of mRNA was quantified with RT-PCR for several 
maj or cytokines, IL- lbeta, -4, -6, -8, - 10, - 12, - 13, - 15 and TNF-alpha, be- 
fore and after delivery of proinflammatory stimuli (IL-lbeta, IFN-gamma 
and TNF-alpha) in fetal and adult myoblasts and SKM14. 
Results: Before proinflammatory stimuli, the expression of IL-lbeta and 
IL-6 mRNA was consistently observed in both types of myoblast. Similar 
levels of IL-12 and IL-15 mRNA expression were detected in fetal my- 
oblast and SKM14, but not in adult myoblast. Weak expression of IL-4 
was found only in adult myoblast. After proinflammatory stimuli, expres- 
sion levels of IL-lbeta, -6, -12 and -15 were enhanced in fetal myoblast 
and SKM14 in a similar manner. Adult myoblast showed a similar ex- 
pression pattern as fetal myoblast or SKM14 except IL-4 and IL-12. The 
proinflammatory stimuli consistently elevated IL-4 expression in adult 
myohlast. 
Conclusion: Overall patterns of cytokine mRNA expression are similar 
across fetal myoblast, adult myoblast and SKM14 cell line, but some 
differences exist in adult myoblast. 
P-469 
Insulin-Like Growth Factor-I Stimulates Calcineurin Activity in L6 
Rat Skeletal Muscle Cells 
E Kanda*, K. Nishimoto, S. Okuda, N. Maeda, H. Ishihara, 
K. Nakazawa, H. Hamaguchi, K. Oishi, K. Sekiguchi, K. Chihara. Kobe, 
Japan 
Objective: Insulin-like growth factor-I (IGF-I) has been shown to induce 
muscle hypertrophy in both physiological and pathological conditions. 
There are two different pathways in IGF-I signal transduction: mitogen- 
activated protein (MAP) kinase pathway and phosphatidylinositol 3 (PI3)- 
kinase pathway. The latter is regarded to be responsible for the anabolic 
effects of IGF-I on muscle. PI3-kinase increases intracellular calcium ion 
concentration to activate calcineurin. Recently, calcineurin has been re- 
ported to be required for skeletal muscle hypertrophy. We studied whether 
IGF-I has possible effects on both expression and activation of calcineurin 
in L6 rat skeletal muscle cell. 
Methods: L6 myoblasts proliferated until they reach confluence and then 
fuse into myotuhes. Differentiated myotuhes are stimulated with IGF-I 
administration in culture medium, thus expression of calcineurin protein 
were measured with immunoblot analysis. Activities of calcineurin in L6

myotubes after IGF-I stimulation were also evaluated by dephosphoryla- 
tion activity. 
Results: IGF-I (750 ng/ml) increased calcineurin expression in L6 rat 
skeletal myotubes. Activity of calcineurin was also enhanced by IGF-I 
administration. 
Conclusion: Hypertrophic effects of IGF-I on skeletal muscle are func- 
tioning through an increase in calcineurin activation. 
P-470 
Cells Expressing Neuronal Markers in Established Primary Mouse 
Myoblast Cultures 
M. Kita*, R. Marotta, A. Quigley, M. Todaro, A. Kornberg, E. Byrne, 
P. Bartlett, S. Morley, R. Kapsa. Melbourne, Australia 
Objective: To investigate myogenic cells' potential to produce neurogenic 
progeny. 
Methods: Pure myoblasts from C57/B6 and mdx mice were derived by 
the pre-plate technique. Slow/non-adhering progeny of these cells were 
propagated and characterized immunohistochemically. 
Results: Adherent cells expressing neuronal markers were observed 
throughout the pre-plate (PP) enrichment of myoblasts. The proportions 
of these cells increased slightly through PP1 to PP5 with approximately 
5-10% of cells in PP5 expressing neuronal markers. In addition, once pure 
myoblasts (100% desmin expressing) were obtained, they produced non- 
adhering, proliferating progeny. Immunohistochemical analysis of these 
cells revealed that the majority were myogenic while a proportion ex- 
pressed neuronal markers. 
Conclusion: These results suggest that a pure population of committed 
myogenic cells in culture may be capable of producing cells with either 
myogenic or neurogenic characteristics. Further studies will evaluate the 
possibility that non-myogenically committed cells of a muscle origin may 
be expanded to provide cells for remodeling muscle tissues. 
P-471 
Establishment of Cell Culture Sytems for the Study of Dysferlin and 
its Interacting Proteins 
S. Laval*, E. Vafiadaki, S. Keers, H. Blair, L. Anderson, K. Bushby. 
Newcastle, UK 
Objectives: Dysferlin is predicted to be a membrane protein containing 6 
C2 domains, indicating a role in membrane fusion events. The objectives 
of this study were to localise dysferlin and the proteins with which it in- 
teracts in cell culture in order to begin to understand their normal function 
and thereby predict the effects of dysferlin deficiency. 
Methods: fusion proteins of dysferlin, caveolin 3, toonin (DYFIP1) and 
calpain 3 with green or red fluorescent protein were expressed in C2C12 
mouse myoblasts cells following differentiation into myotubes and the 
localisation of these proteins assessed by fluorescence and confocal mi- 
croscopy. 
Results: dysferlin expression was localised to a novel class of intracel- 
lular vesicles during myoblast differentiation. This expression coincided 
with the pattern observed for DYSFIP1 in the peri-nuclear region but was 
distinct from caveolin-3. 
Conclusions: These results have to be interpreted in the context of find- 
ings in animal models of dysferlinopathy and in patients with LGMD2B/ 
Miyoshi myopathy. However, these observations predict that dysferlin is 
involved in a number of different steps during the reorganisation of the 
internal membranous compartments of the developing myoblast. 
P-472 
Study of Non-Adherent Ceils During Preplating of Muscle Cultures 
R. Marotta*, M. Kita, M. Todaro, A. Quigely, A. Kornberg, E. Byrne, 
R. Kapsa. Melbourne, Australia 
Objective: To investigate the propagation and expansion of myoblast cul- 
tures for autologous cell transplantation.

Methods: Using the mdx mouse model, myogenic cells were propagated 
and evaluated for expansion in primary cultures beyond preplate 6 (PP6). 
Results: Adherent mouse myoblasts were obtained in addition to a non- 
adherent subpopulation of cells in preplates beyond PP6. Immunohisto- 
chemistry indicated that the non-adherent cells from later preplates con- 
tained non-adherent subpopulations of desmin and non-desmin expressing 
cells, in addition to a pure population of adherent committed desmin pos- 
itive cells. Differentiation of the adherent myogenic cells into myotuhes 
gave rise to a further population of non-adherent cells similar to that

Poster Presentations Wednesday, July 10, 2002 $81 
observed originally. Under non-differentiating conditions, these cells sub- 
divided into adherent and non-adherent populations. The non-adherent 
subpopulation retained desmin positive and negative cells whereas the 
adherent cells were all desmin positive. 
Conclusion: These results suggest that the myogenic commitment of cells 
derived from muscle may be altered during culture and that such cells may 
be expanded to generate large numbers of myogenic cells for transplanta- 
tion. 
P-473 
Up-Regulation of Chemokine-Like Factor in Cultured Myoblasts 
Following Treatment with Thrombin 
A. Nagai, Y. Ishida, S. Kobayashi. Izumo, Japan 
Objectives: Thrombosis is known to occur during atherogenesis and in 
response to vascular injury. Growing evidence supports a role for inflam- 
mation of thrombosis under the same condition. To examine the rela- 
tionship between thrombosis and inflammation, we investigated whether 
thrombin, which is present in active form at sites of thrombosis, can elicit 
inflammatory functions in cultured human myocytes. 
Methods: Human muscle satellite cells were cultured using muscle biop- 
sies from the patients with neuromascular diseases after informed consent. 
The expression of protease activated receptors was examined by RT-PCR. 
Cultured myohlasts at the second passage were treated with thromhin and 
then expression of cathepsin B and chemokine-like factor 1 (CKLF1) was 
examined by RT-PCR. 
Results: The expression of protease activated receptor-1 was detected in 
cultured myoblasts by RT-PCR. Expression of cathepsin B in myoblasts 
was up-regulated following treatment with thrombin in a dose-dependent 
manner, which suggests that thrombin induces an increase in protease 
activity in myoblasts. Expression of a secreted type of novel chemokine, 
chemokine-like factor 1 (CKLF1) was also up-regulated in myoblasts. 
Conclusion: These results suggest that thrombin may be involved in in- 
flammation of muscle by means of up-regulating protease activities and 
promoting a chemoattractant. 
P-474 
WNT3A and GLI2 are Necessary and Sufficient for Skeletal 
Myogenesis 
I. Skerjanc*, H. Petropoulos. London, Canada 
Objective: The Gli2 zinc finger transcription factor and the Wnt3a signal- 
ing molecule play important roles in early somitogenesis. Our objective 
was to determine their roles in the molecular cascade of events regulating 
myogenic regulatory factor (MRF) expression during myogenesis. 
Methods: Our approach was to isolate stable P19 cell lines overexpressing 
wild type or dominant negative forms of Gli2 (Gli2/EnR) or beta-catenin 
(B-cat/EnR) and to examine their function during cellular aggregation. 
Results: Overexpression of either Wnt3a or Gli2 induced myogenesis 
and the expression of the transcription factors Pax3, Moxl, and MRFs in 
cells aggregated in the absence of DMSO. Overexpression of Wnt3a also 
induced the expression of Gli2. Overexpression of either Gli2/EnR or B- 
cat/EnR completely abolished skeletal myogenesis and MRF expression 
in P19 cells aggregated in the presence of DMSO. Overexpression of 
B-cat/EnR resulted in a loss of expression of Pax3, Gli2, and Moxl. 
Overexpression of Gli2/EnR down-regulated Mox 1 but did not affect the 
expression of Pax3. 
Conclusions: The combined approach of expressing both wild type and 
dominant negative transcription factors in stem cells has identified a cas-

cade of transcriptional events, initiated by Wnt3a and controlled by Gli2, 
that are necessary and sufficient for skeletal myogenesis. 
P-475 
Experimental Verification of Bioinformatic Predictions using the 
MYH Family of Muscle-Specific Promoters 
Hansell Stedman, James Burkman, Doug Stewart, Stephane Konig. 
Department of Surgery, University of Pennsylvania Medical Cente~ 
Philadelphia, PA 19104, USA 
We have used a combination of phylogenetic fingerprinting, matrix-based 
prediction of DNA-protein interactions, in vitro transfection and in vivo 
electroporation to map conserved cis-acting elements that contribute to 
the activation of the powerful, muscle-specific MYH promoters. A "top 
down" experimental approach has been used to localize regions involved 
in promoter activation. One region of particular interest from the MYH 3 
promoter cross activates, in cis, each of the other tandemly linked MYH 
minimal promoters. Ultimately, a minimal length construct (400 bp) com- 
bining selected proximal and distal regions rich in putative MyoD and 
MEF2 binding sites reconstituted the extraordinary strength of an ex- 
tended region spanning 20 kb upstream of the transcriptional start site. 
Further studies involving site-directed mutagenesis and reversion estab- 
lish the critical role of the putative MyoD and MEF2 sites. Comparison 
and alignment of paralogous gene sequences has enabled the identifi- 
cation of consensus proximal promoter sequences with the finding that 
subtle differences in the position and "strength" of the most proximal 
MEF-2 site correlate with the developmental stage of promoter activation. 
These studies may shed light on the fiber type disproportion syndromes 
and should provide exceptionally powerful transcriptional cassettes for a 
range of applications in gene therapy for neuromuscular diseases. 
P-476 
Gene Expression Analysis in Differentiating C2C12 Ceils 
K. Tomczak*, D. Sanoudou, M. Han, I.S. Kohane, A.H. Beggs. Boston, 
USA 
We used expression profiling to develop a catalog of genes induced in dif- 
ferentiating mouse C2C12 myoblasts. Day 0 proliferating cells were in- 
duced to differentiate through addition of fusion media. Triplicate cultures 
were harvested on days -2, -1, 0, 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10, for target preparation. 
We analyzed expression patterns of 12,422 probe sets using Affymetrix 
MG U74Av.2 oligonucleotide microarrays. T-test, fold comparisons and 
cluster analysis are being performed to identify genes with coordinate 
expression patterns and/or variable expression levels between differenti- 
ating and proliferating cells. 4241 probe sets were called "absent" in all 
data sets. 69 probe sets were scored "marginally present" or better in all 
proliferating cultures and "absent" in all differentiated ones. Conversely, 
150 genes were turned on in fusing cells only. 471 and 367 genes were 
up- and down-regulated respectively by >3 fold over the time course. 
106 were induced > 10 fold. The vast majority of these represent known 
muscle-specific genes. For instance 27% were sarcomeric with 11 myosin 
genes and 8 troponins. Nine genes were unknown and they may be studied 
more carefully in the future. Ongoing studies are extending this data set to 
include another 12,000 ESTs to allow identification of new differentiation- 
induced transcripts 
P-477 
The Formation Process of Integrin Over-Expressed in Growing 
Quail Myotubes 
T. Toursel*, H.S. Feng, H.L. Sweeney. Philadelphia, PA, USA

Integrin ct7B1, the principal integrin receptor on skeletal muscles, bridge 
the extracellular matrix to the cytoskeleton. Integrin is essential for func- 
tional and structural integrity of muscles, as suggested by its roles in cells 
growth, differentiation and motility. In the present study, we cloned in 
the expression vector pRc/CMV the ct7B and B1D-Integrins DNAs fused 
with GFP or myc-tag for transfection in using the cell culture system 
of quail embryonic pectoral myoblasts. Polyclonal anti-ct7B and anti- 
BID; monoclonal anti-BID and anti-myc were used with DAPi to stain 
the myoblasts and myotubes of day 5, 8 and 12 cultures. Preparations

$82 Wednesday, July 10, 2002 Poster Presentations 
were examined by Leica DMR fluorescence microscope and Princeton 
Instrument for imaging. Peri-nucleus ct7B or ~31D distribution shows in 
the early stage mono-nucleus and spindle-like myoblasts. In the longer 
spindle-like mono-nucleus myoblasts, vesicles can be seen surrounded 
close to nucleus. Diffused integrins spread in myoblasts after fusing and 
also in young myotubes. On day 5, integrin starts to organize and stained 
in periodic bands, which can be co-stained with anti-ct-actinin antibody. 
Finally, [31D-integrin incorporated the membrane when myotubes getting 
fully matured. In conclusion, exogenous integrin can incorporate the mem- 
brane. We are now testing whether or not it provides a reinforced linkage 
system to improve membrane strength in muscular dystrophies wherein 
the dystrophin complex is absent. 
P-478 
Proliferative Plasticity of Satellite Cells 
Z. Yablonka-Reuveni*. Seattle, USA 
We have been investigating mechanisms that support stem-like character- 
istics of satellite cells in mature muscle. We showed that selective fibrob- 
last growth factors (FGFs) regulate the short-term proliferative capacity 
of satellite cells in myofibers from adult rodents. However, in this culture 
model the satellite cells rapidly differentiate. In contrast, progeny of satel- 
lite cells in myofibers from mice lacking MyoD continue to proliferate for 
a long time before they differentiate. Hence, MyoD may act as a regulatory 
switch of proliferative plasticity in vivo; the repression of MyoD activity 
may allow satellite cells to function as self-renewed stem cells while the 
activation of MyoD may enforce a limited proliferation and rapid differ- 
entiation. We have also investigated the proliferative potential of satellite 
cells in myofibers from very old mice (34-month-old). In this case the 
satellite cells are unable to enter short-term proliferation without the addi- 
tion of FGF2. However, satellite cells from old mice are clonable, prolifer- 
ate extensively, and produce numerous differentiation-able progeny when 
dissociated from the muscle and cultured in a serum-rich/mitogen-rich 
environment. Hence, satellite cells maintain their stem-like characteristics 
even at the end of the life span.

P-479 
Genome-Wide Profiles of Developing Musde: Patterned 
Extraocular-Leg Differences in Rate-Limiting and Disease-Related 
Metabolic Enzyme Expression 
G. Cheng*, S. Khanna, A.P. Merriam, P. Leahy, EH. Andrade, 
J.D. Porter. Cleveland, USA 
Objective: Identify gene expression patterns behind the unique proper- 
ties/disease responsiveness of extraocular muscle (EOM). 
Methods: Gene profiling assessed development of rat EOM (P0-P45) and 
leg (E18-P45) muscles. 
Results: 3318 and 4356 were expressed with >2x changes during de- 
velopment of EOM and leg, respectively. Specific major EOM themes in 
energy metabolism transcripts included: (a) shared perinatal patterns, fol- 
lowed by EOM-leg divergence (e.g., Hkl, Hk2, Scdl, Scd2), (b) retention 
of otherwise developmentally repressed isoforms or reliance on alternate, 
non-muscle, isoforms (e.g., Pfkp/Pfkm, Pgaml/Pgam2), and (c) low ex- 
pression of some enzyme isoforms linked to metabolic myopathies (e.g., 
Amdl, Pfkm, Pgam2, G6ptl). Expression data also suggested that EOM 
may use unidentified, non-muscle isoforms of Pgml and Pfkfb (glycoly-

sis), G6pd (pentose shunt), and Amd 1 (purine cycle). Glycogen regulation 
mRNAs (Phakl, Calm, Phkgl, Gyg) were differentially expressed, con- 
sistent with low EOM glycogen content. 
Conclusions: Data establish a broad developmental framework behind 
the novel EOM phenotype. Use of embryonic/alternative metabolic en- 
zyme isoforms in EOM, a strategy having undetermined functional con- 
sequences, suggests that EOM utilizes the full range of skeletal muscle 
options, and then some. Given that EOM is refractory to many muscle 
diseases, the low expression of transcripts linked to metabolic myopathies 
is particularly intriguing. 
P-480 
Developmental Expression of Syntrophin and Dystrobrevin in 
Human Skeletal Muscle 
A.G. Compton* 1,2, S.T. Cooper 1, M.F. Peters 3 , L.M. Kunkel 4 , 
S.C. Froehner 3 , K.N. North 1,2. llnst" for Neuromuscular Research, The 
Children's Hospital at Westmead, Sydney; :Dept. of Paediatrics and 
Child Health, Univ. of Sydney, Australia; 3Dept. of Physiology and 
Biophysics, Univ. of Washington, Seattle, WA; 4Howard Hughes Medical 
Inst., Children's Hospital and Harvard Medical Sch., Boston, MA, USA 
Previous work in our laboratory has identified a cohort of congenital my- 
opathy patients with isolated deficiency in the syntrophin/dystrobrevin 
complex [1], which interact with the dystrophin-associated-protein com- 
plex (DAPC) at the sarcolemmal membrane and at the neuromuscular 
junction (NMJ). Since normal expression of the syntrophins and dystro- 
brevins has been defined only in mouse, we aimed to determine the local- 
ization and developmental expression of these proteins in human muscle 
and cultured myotubes, and to explore their role as potential candidates as 
primary causes of muscle disease. 
The developmental expression of cd-syntrophin, [51-syntrophin, [52-syn- 
trophin, ct-dystrobrevin-1 and ct-dystrobrevin-2 were examined using iso- 
form specific antibodies in human developmental samples ranging from 19 
weeks gestation through to 8 years of age and in primary human myoblasts 
(throughout myogenic differentiation). Both protein families showed ex- 
pression early in development (19 weeks gestation in muscle samples) 
through to maturity. In general, the expression patterns of the different 
proteins showed localization similar to that published in murine muscle 
except [52-syntrophin expression which localized to both the sarcolemma 
of type I fibres as well as the NMJ. Further cell culture studies aim to char- 
acterize the intracellular trafficking of the syntrophins and dystrobrevins 
to further delineate their roles in the DAPC and NMJ complexes. 
References 
[1] Jones KJ, Compton AG, Mills MM, et al. (2002). Submitted. 
P-481 
Obscurin Interacts with Skeletal Muscle Specific Filamin 
I. Dalkilic .1 , T.G. Thompson I , M.A. Brossius I , A.A. Puca 1, C. Feener 1, 
F. Muntoni 2, L.M. Kunkel 1. 1Boston, USA; :London, UK 
Objective: Skeletal muscle specific y-filamin interacts with ~- and y- 
sarcoglycans, y-filamin localizes to both the sarcolemmal membrane and 
cytoplasm. In patients with sarcoglycanopathies, the percentage of y- 
filamin in the membrane is greatly increased. To better understand the 
role of y-filamin in skeletal muscle we have performed a yeast two-hybrid 
assay to find novel interacting partners. 
Methods: We have used the C-terminus of y-filamin to screen a skeletal 
muscle cDNA library in a GAL4 based yeast two hybrid system. We

have utilized in vitro transcription translation to co-immunoprecipitate 
y-filamin with obscurin. We have generated antibodies and studied the 
expression pattern of obscurin. 
Results: Obscurin interacts with y-filamin in both assays used. Obscurin 
is a large muscle specific protein (>700 kD) and localizes to the M-line 
in skeletal muscle fibers. The obscurin gene has an open reading frame of 
23 000, 87 exons and maps to lq42. It has been reported congenital mus- 
cular dystrophy (CMD1B) are genetically is linked to a region containing 
obscurin. We have also determined the genomic organization for obscurin 
and generated primers to screen patients. 
Conclusions: We have demonstrated that y-filamin interacts with obscurin 
both in vitro and in yeast two hybrid system. Genomic localization of the 
gene makes it a candidate for CMD lB. We are currently screening patients 
with CMD lB.

Stiff Person Syndrome (SPS): A Pediatric Case Report 
N.S. Shah .1 , A. Hahn 2, B. Banwell 1. 1Toronto, Canada; 2London, 
Canada 
Introduction: SPS is a rare disorder characterized by fluctuating muscle 
rigidity and spasms. Most patients present in adulthood. We report a case 
with onset at 8 years, review of reported pediatric cases, and discuss 
various therapeutic modalities. 
Clinical evulation: A previously healthy, athletic 8 year old girl had onset 
of severe episodes of pain in lower back and legs. Recurrent, episodic mus- 
cle stiffness precipitated by loud noise and tactile stimulation lasting 3 to 
5 minutes, occurred multiple times per day. Examination during episodes 
revealed muscle stiffness with extreme pain with hyperreflexia. Reduced 
lumbar extension and subjective stiffness in lower paraspinal muscles 
without myotonia was evident between attacks. MRI head, CSF stud- 
ies, evoked potentials, and electromyography (performed when asymp- 
tomatic) were normal. Serum studies performed by the Mayo Clinic 
demonstrated GAD-65 (glutamic acid decarboxylase) antibody titres of 
0.13(normal = 0.02). Serum glucose and thyroid function were normal. 
Treatment: High dose corticosteroids significantly improved muscle 
spasms during attacks. The frequency of attacks was markedly reduced 
with monthly IVIg infusions and muscle stiffness has improved on main- 
tenance regime of Tizanidine and Gabapentin. 
Discussion: SPS is presumed to have an autoimmune pathogenesis, based 
on presence of GAD autoantibodies and association with other autoim- 
mune or paraneoplastic disorders. SPS is extremely rare in the pediatric 
population. The 8 cases described in the literature will be reviewed. The 
management of the present case highlights the need for multisymptomatic 
therapy.
